items.title: Citi sees early signs of energy pass through By Investing.com
items.excerpt: Investing.com -- Citi told clients in a note Tuesday that October’s consumer price data may offer the clearest signs yet that higher energy and transport costs are filtering through to other prices, though it cautioned that more data is needed to confirm the trend. Core CPI rose 0.3% in October, the third straight month of stronger-than-expected readings. Citi now expects core PCE inflation, the Fed’s preferred gauge, to rise to 3.2% year over year in October. “Some details of October data may offer the clearest signs yet that higher input and transportation costs are pushing up other prices,” the bank wrote. October showed unusually large increases in household furnishings, restaurants, medical goods, car insurance and local transport such as taxis. Citi said higher taxi fares very likely reflect gas prices, while stronger furnishings prices may reflect higher shipping costs. ... Citi expects the next four months of inflation data to be strong, though it sees downside risks to high expectations in the first quarter. Factors that boosted early 2026 inflation, such as airfares, may be weaker this time. “If rising prices do reflect more energy price pass-through, we would expect some stickiness to stronger increases, with prices continuing to rise over the next few months,” the bank added.

items.title: Dollar holds near 19-month high as data supports case for US rate hikes By Reuters
items.excerpt: TOKYO, Nov 18 (Reuters) - The dollar held steady near a 19-month high on Wednesday as US economic data and comments from Federal Reserve officials lent support to the case for interest rate hikes. The yen held its ground after Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda reiterated the need to tighten policy further. The Australian dollar languished near a 10-month low ahead of a key jobs report on Thursday. Data on Tuesday showed US retail sales increased moderately in October, reinforcing expectations for a rate hike next month. Attention turns to US housing starts data due later on Wednesday as well as a series of Fed speakers, all ahead of the Thursday release of minutes of the central bank’s meeting last month when it held rates steady. "Overall, the report reinforces our view that further interest rate hikes from the Fed are warranted in order to counter demand-pull inflation," Henry Russell, a London-based economist for ANZ, said about the US sales data. "The strength of domestic demand in the US, in our view, warrants a decisive monetary policy response from the Fed." The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, rose 0.04% to 103.65. It touched 103.78 overnight, its highest level since April 2, 2025. The euro was down 0.1% at $1.0986, while the yen was flat at 159.35 per dollar. Sterling lost 0.11% to $1.3193. In addition to a 0.2% rise in retail sales that matched expectations, import prices climbed 1.1% in October compared with expectations for a 0.7% increase. More US data is expected with the Census Bureau due to report housing starts data for October. Analysts are projecting an increase to 1.245 million from 1.221 million in September, while building permits likely decreased. New York Fed President John Williams is expected to speak again following comments on Tuesday when he said the Fed will likely need to raise interest rates further to contend with inflation. Fed Board Governor Michael Barr and Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari are also expected to speak at separate events. Traders are pricing in a 95.7% chance that the Fed will raise its key rate by 25 basis points (bps) in December, the CME FedWatch tool showed. The odds of a 50-bp increase have fallen from 13.5% a month ago to 4.3% currently.
